question: Prove that if a function $f$ is continuous on $[a, b]$, then it is Riemann integrable on $[a, b]$.
approach: Use Heine-Cantor theorem (continuous on compact $[a, b]$ is uniformly continuous) and Riemann's criterion.

solution_steps.title: Uniform Continuity on Compact Interval
solution_steps.math: f \in C[a, b] \implies f \text{ is uniformly continuous on } [a, b]
solution_steps.explanation: Since $[a, b]$ is closed and bounded, continuity implies uniform continuity.

solution_steps.title: Choosing Partition Mesh
solution_steps.math: \forall \epsilon > 0, \; \exists \delta > 0 : |x - y| < \delta \implies |f(x) - f(y)| < \frac{\epsilon}{b - a}
solution_steps.explanation: By uniform continuity.

solution_steps.title: Oscillation on Subintervals
solution_steps.math: \|P\| < \delta \implies M_i - m_i = f(u_i) - f(v_i) < \frac{\epsilon}{b - a}
solution_steps.explanation: Since $f$ attains its supremum $M_i$ and infimum $m_i$ on $[x_{i-1}, x_i]$ at some points $u_i, v_i$.

solution_steps.title: Darboux Sum Difference
solution_steps.math: U(P, f) - L(P, f) = \sum_{i=1}^n (M_i - m_i)\Delta x_i < \frac{\epsilon}{b-a} \sum_{i=1}^n \Delta x_i = \frac{\epsilon}{b-a}(b - a) = \epsilon
solution_steps.explanation: By Riemann's Criterion, $f$ is Riemann integrable.

final_answer: Every continuous function on a closed bounded interval $[a, b]$ is Riemann integrable.
exam_tip: Explicitly invoke the Heine-Cantor Theorem: continuity on a compact interval implies uniform continuity.

question: State and prove the Integration by Parts formula for Riemann integrals.
approach: Integrate the product rule derivative $(fg)' = f'g + fg'$ using the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus.

solution_steps.title: Statement
solution_steps.math: f, g \in C^1[a, b] \implies \int_a^b f(x) g'(x) dx = [f(x)g(x)]_a^b - \int_a^b f'(x) g(x) dx
solution_steps.explanation: Integration by parts formula for Riemann integrals.

solution_steps.title: Product Rule of Differentiation
solution_steps.math: (fg)'(x) = f'(x)g(x) + f(x)g'(x) \quad \forall x \in [a, b]
solution_steps.explanation: Since $f$ and $g$ are differentiable.

solution_steps.title: Integration and Linearity
solution_steps.math: \int_a^b (fg)'(x) dx = \int_a^b f'(x)g(x) dx + \int_a^b f(x)g'(x) dx
solution_steps.explanation: Integrating both sides from $a$ to $b$.

solution_steps.title: Application of Fundamental Theorem of Calculus
solution_steps.math: \int_a^b (fg)'(x) dx = [f(x)g(x)]_a^b = f(b)g(b) - f(a)g(a)
solution_steps.explanation: Rearranging gives the desired formula.

final_answer: $\int_a^b f g' = f(b)g(b) - f(a)g(a) - \int_a^b f' g$.
exam_tip: Make sure to state that both $f'$ and $g'$ must be Riemann integrable on $[a, b]$.

question: State and prove the Second Fundamental Theorem of Calculus.
concept_tested: Second Fundamental Theorem of Calculus (Evaluation Theorem)
approach: Let $F$ be an antiderivative ($F' = f$), use Mean Value Theorem on each subinterval $[x_{i-1}, x_i]$, and squeeze between Darboux sums.

solution_steps.title: Statement
solution_steps.math: f \in \mathcal{R}[a, b] \land F'(x) = f(x) \; \forall x \in [a, b] \implies \int_a^b f(x) dx = F(b) - F(a)
solution_steps.explanation: If $f$ is Riemann integrable and has an antiderivative $F$, then the integral equals the total change in $F$.

solution_steps.title: Telescoping Sum & Mean Value Theorem
solution_steps.math: F(b) - F(a) = \sum_{i=1}^n [F(x_i) - F(x_{i-1})] = \sum_{i=1}^n F'(t_i)\Delta x_i = \sum_{i=1}^n f(t_i)\Delta x_i
solution_steps.explanation: By Lagrange's MVT on each subinterval $[x_{i-1}, x_i]$, there exists $t_i \in (x_{i-1}, x_i)$ such that $F(x_i) - F(x_{i-1}) = F'(t_i)\Delta x_i$.

solution_steps.title: Trapping between Darboux Sums
solution_steps.math: m_i \le f(t_i) \le M_i \implies L(P, f) \le F(b) - F(a) \le U(P, f) \quad \forall P
solution_steps.explanation: Since $F(b) - F(a)$ is trapped between $L(P, f)$ and $U(P, f)$ for every partition $P$.

solution_steps.title: Conclusion
solution_steps.math: \sup_P L(P, f) \le F(b) - F(a) \le \inf_P U(P, f) \implies \int_a^b f(x) dx = F(b) - F(a)
solution_steps.explanation: Since $f \in \mathcal{R}[a, b]$, the upper and lower integrals coincide and equal $\int_a^b f$.

exam_tip: The telescoping MVT argument is the standard rigorous proof in Bartle & Sherbert Theorem 7.3.1.

question: If $f$ is monotonic on $[a, b]$, show that $f$ is Riemann integrable on $[a, b]$.
approach: Partition into $n$ equal subintervals; telescoping sum cancels internal terms.

solution_steps.title: Partition Setup
solution_steps.math: \Delta x_i = \frac{b - a}{n} \quad \forall i = 1, \dots, n
solution_steps.explanation: Choose a uniform partition $P_n$ of $[a, b]$ into $n$ equal parts.

solution_steps.title: Subinterval Extrema for Increasing Function
solution_steps.math: m_i = f(x_{i-1}), \quad M_i = f(x_i) \implies M_i - m_i = f(x_i) - f(x_{i-1})
solution_steps.explanation: Because $f$ is monotonically increasing.

solution_steps.title: Telescoping Darboux Difference
solution_steps.math: U(P_n, f) - L(P_n, f) = \sum_{i=1}^n [f(x_i) - f(x_{i-1})] \frac{b - a}{n} = \frac{b - a}{n} [f(b) - f(a)]
solution_steps.explanation: The sum telescopes to $f(b) - f(a)$.

solution_steps.title: Riemann Criterion Verification
solution_steps.math: \forall \epsilon > 0, \text{ choose } n > \frac{(b-a)[f(b)-f(a)]}{\epsilon} \implies U(P_n, f) - L(P_n, f) < \epsilon
solution_steps.explanation: By the Archimedean Property, such $n$ exists. Hence $f \in \mathcal{R}[a, b]$.

final_answer: Every monotonic function on $[a, b]$ is Riemann integrable.
exam_tip: Note that monotonic functions may have countably many discontinuities and are still Riemann integrable!

question: State and prove the Riemann Criterion for integrability of a bounded function.
approach: Prove both directions: $(\implies)$ integrability implies $U - L < \epsilon$; $(\impliedby)$ $U - L < \epsilon$ implies $\overline{\int} = \underline{\int}$.

solution_steps.title: Direction 1 ($\implies$): Integrability $\implies$ Criterion
solution_steps.math: \underline{\int_a^b} f = \overline{\int_a^b} f = I. \quad \exists P_1 : L(P_1, f) > I - \frac{\epsilon}{2}, \quad \exists P_2 : U(P_2, f) < I + \frac{\epsilon}{2}
solution_steps.explanation: By definitions of supremum and infimum.

solution_steps.title: Common Refinement $P = P_1 \cup P_2$
solution_steps.math: U(P, f) - L(P, f) \le U(P_2, f) - L(P_1, f) < \left(I + \frac{\epsilon}{2}\right) - \left(I - \frac{\epsilon}{2}\right) = \epsilon
solution_steps.explanation: Refinement decreases upper sums and increases lower sums.

solution_steps.title: Direction 2 ($\impliedby$): Criterion $\implies$ Integrability
solution_steps.math: L(P, f) \le \underline{\int_a^b} f \le \overline{\int_a^b} f \le U(P, f) \implies 0 \le \overline{\int_a^b} f - \underline{\int_a^b} f \le U(P, f) - L(P, f) < \epsilon
solution_steps.explanation: Since this holds for every $\epsilon > 0$, the non-negative quantity $\overline{\int} f - \underline{\int} f$ must equal 0.

final_answer: $f \in \mathcal{R}[a, b] \iff \forall \epsilon > 0, \exists P_\epsilon \text{ s.t. } U(P_\epsilon, f) - L(P_\epsilon, f) < \epsilon$.
exam_tip: The common refinement $P = P_1 \cup P_2$ is essential in the forward direction.

question: Prove that every continuous function on $[a, b]$ is Riemann integrable.
approach: Use uniform continuity on $[a, b]$: $\forall \epsilon > 0, \exists \delta > 0: |x-y| < \delta \implies |f(x) - f(y)| < \frac{\epsilon}{b-a}$.

solution_steps.title: Uniform Continuity
solution_steps.math: f \in C[a, b] \implies f \text{ is uniformly continuous on } [a, b]
solution_steps.explanation: Continuous function on a closed bounded interval is uniformly continuous.

solution_steps.title: Partition with $\|P\| < \delta$
solution_steps.math: x, y \in [x_{i-1}, x_i] \implies |x - y| \le \|P\| < \delta \implies |f(x) - f(y)| < \frac{\epsilon}{b - a}
solution_steps.explanation: Given $\epsilon > 0$, choose partition $P$ with $\|P\| < \delta$.

solution_steps.title: Sum Difference
solution_steps.math: M_i - m_i = f(u_i) - f(v_i) \le \frac{\epsilon}{b-a} \implies U(P, f) - L(P, f) = \sum_{i=1}^n (M_i - m_i)\Delta x_i < \epsilon
solution_steps.explanation: Since $f$ attains extreme values at $u_i, v_i$.

final_answer: By Riemann's criterion, $f$ is Riemann integrable on $[a, b]$.
exam_tip: Uniform continuity is the key ingredient that lets us choose a single $\delta$ across the whole interval.

question: Prove that every monotonic function on $[a, b]$ is Riemann integrable.
approach: Telescoping sum with uniform partition of $n$ subintervals.

solution_steps.title: Uniform Partition
solution_steps.math: P_n = \{x_0, x_1, \dots, x_n\}, \quad \Delta x_i = \frac{b - a}{n}
solution_steps.explanation: Divide $[a, b]$ into $n$ equal segments.

solution_steps.title: Darboux Sum Difference
solution_steps.math: U(P_n, f) - L(P_n, f) = \sum_{i=1}^n (f(x_i) - f(x_{i-1})) \frac{b-a}{n} = \frac{b-a}{n}(f(b) - f(a))
solution_steps.explanation: Sum telescopes completely.

solution_steps.title: Choosing $n$
solution_steps.math: n > \frac{(b-a)(f(b)-f(a))}{\epsilon} \implies U(P_n, f) - L(P_n, f) < \epsilon
solution_steps.explanation: Thus $f$ satisfies Riemann's criterion.

final_answer: Every monotonic function on $[a, b]$ is Riemann integrable.
exam_tip: If $f(a) = f(b)$, $f$ is constant and the result is trivial.

question: Let $f(x) = x$ on $[0, 1]$. Using partitions into equal subintervals, find the Riemann integral $\int_0^1 x dx$.
concept_tested: Direct Computation of Riemann Integral via Upper/Lower Sums
approach: Use uniform partition of $[0, 1]$ into $n$ parts for $f(x) = x$, compute $U(P_n)$ and $L(P_n)$, and take limit as $n \to \infty$.

solution_steps.title: Partition Setup
solution_steps.math: P_n = \left\{0, \frac{1}{n}, \frac{2}{n}, \dots, \frac{n}{n} = 1\right\}, \quad \Delta x_i = \frac{1}{n}
solution_steps.explanation: Subintervals are $[\frac{i-1}{n}, \frac{i}{n}]$.

solution_steps.title: Upper Sum $U(P_n, f)$
solution_steps.math: M_i = f\left(\frac{i}{n}\right) = \frac{i}{n} \implies U(P_n, f) = \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{i}{n} \cdot \frac{1}{n} = \frac{1}{n^2} \frac{n(n+1)}{2} = \frac{n+1}{2n} = \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{2n}
solution_steps.explanation: Using the formula $\sum_{i=1}^n i = \frac{n(n+1)}{2}$.

solution_steps.title: Lower Sum $L(P_n, f)$
solution_steps.math: m_i = f\left(\frac{i-1}{n}\right) = \frac{i-1}{n} \implies L(P_n, f) = \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{i-1}{n} \cdot \frac{1}{n} = \frac{1}{n^2} \frac{(n-1)n}{2} = \frac{n-1}{2n} = \frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{2n}
solution_steps.explanation: Using $\sum_{i=1}^n (i-1) = \frac{(n-1)n}{2}$.

solution_steps.title: Limit as $n \to \infty$
solution_steps.math: \lim_{n \to \infty} U(P_n, f) = \lim_{n \to \infty} L(P_n, f) = \frac{1}{2} \implies \int_0^1 x dx = \frac{1}{2}
solution_steps.explanation: Both upper and lower sums converge to $1/2$.

exam_tip: Explicitly state the summation identities used: $\sum_{i=1}^n i = \frac{n(n+1)}{2}$.

question: Show that Dirichlet's function $f(x) = 1$ if $x \in \mathbb{Q}$ and $f(x) = 0$ if $x \notin \mathbb{Q}$ is not Riemann integrable on $[0, 1]$.
approach: Compute upper and lower integrals using density of $\mathbb{Q}$ and $\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q}$.

solution_steps.title: Subinterval Sup and Inf
solution_steps.math: f(x) = \begin{cases} 1, & x \in \mathbb{Q} \\ 0, & x \notin \mathbb{Q} \end{cases} \implies M_i = \sup_{I_i} f = 1, \quad m_i = \inf_{I_i} f = 0
solution_steps.explanation: Every non-empty open subinterval contains both rational and irrational numbers.

solution_steps.title: Darboux Sums for Any Partition $P$
solution_steps.math: U(P, f) = \sum_{i=1}^n 1 \cdot \Delta x_i = 1(1 - 0) = 1, \qquad L(P, f) = \sum_{i=1}^n 0 \cdot \Delta x_i = 0
solution_steps.explanation: These hold identically for every partition $P$.

solution_steps.title: Comparison of Integrals
solution_steps.math: \overline{\int_0^1} f = \inf_P U(P, f) = 1 \ne 0 = \sup_P L(P, f) = \underline{\int_0^1} f
solution_steps.explanation: Since the upper and lower integrals are not equal, $f$ is not Riemann integrable.

final_answer: Dirichlet's function is not Riemann integrable on $[0, 1]$ because $\underline{\int} f = 0 \ne 1 = \overline{\int} f$.
exam_tip: Cite the Density Theorems for $\mathbb{Q}$ and $\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q}$ as the rigorous justification.

question: Prove that if $f$ and $g$ are Riemann integrable on $[a, b]$, then $f + g$ is Riemann integrable on $[a, b]$ and $\int_a^b (f+g) = \int_a^b f + \int_a^b g$.
approach: Use tagged Riemann sums or Darboux sums and the inequality $m_i(f) + m_i(g) \le m_i(f+g) \le M_i(f+g) \le M_i(f) + M_i(g)$.

solution_steps.title: Subinterval Bounds
solution_steps.math: m_i(f) + m_i(g) \le m_i(f+g) \le M_i(f+g) \le M_i(f) + M_i(g)
solution_steps.explanation: By properties of supremum and infimum.

solution_steps.title: Sum Inequalities
solution_steps.math: L(P, f) + L(P, g) \le L(P, f+g) \le U(P, f+g) \le U(P, f) + U(P, g)
solution_steps.explanation: Multiplying by $\Delta x_i$ and summing over $i$.

solution_steps.title: Riemann Criterion for $f+g$
solution_steps.math: U(P, f+g) - L(P, f+g) \le [U(P, f) - L(P, f)] + [U(P, g) - L(P, g)] < \frac{\epsilon}{2} + \frac{\epsilon}{2} = \epsilon
solution_steps.explanation: Choosing common partition where both $f$ and $g$ have Darboux differences $< \epsilon/2$.

solution_steps.title: Integral Value
solution_steps.math: \int_a^b (f+g) = \int_a^b f + \int_a^b g
solution_steps.explanation: Since the integral is squeezed between $L(P, f) + L(P, g)$ and $U(P, f) + U(P, g)$.

exam_tip: Note that $U(P, f+g) \le U(P, f) + U(P, g)$ follows from subadditivity of the supremum.

question: Show that if $f$ is Riemann integrable on $[a, b]$, then $|f|$ is Riemann integrable and $|\int_a^b f| \le \int_a^b |f|$.
approach: Use reverse triangle inequality $||f(x)| - |f(y)|| \le |f(x) - f(y)|$ to bound oscillations, then $-|f| \le f \le |f|$.

solution_steps.title: Oscillation Bound
solution_steps.math: M_i(|f|) - m_i(|f|) = \sup_{x, y \in I_i} ||f(x)| - |f(y)|| \le \sup_{x, y \in I_i} |f(x) - f(y)| = M_i(f) - m_i(f)
solution_steps.explanation: The oscillation of $|f|$ on any interval never exceeds the oscillation of $f$.

solution_steps.title: Darboux Difference
solution_steps.math: U(P, |f|) - L(P, |f|) \le U(P, f) - L(P, f) < \epsilon
solution_steps.explanation: Hence $|f|$ satisfies the Riemann Criterion and is integrable.

solution_steps.title: Integral Inequality
solution_steps.math: -|f(x)| \le f(x) \le |f(x)| \implies -\int_a^b |f| \le \int_a^b f \le \int_a^b |f| \iff \left|\int_a^b f\right| \le \int_a^b |f|
solution_steps.explanation: By monotonicity of the Riemann integral.

exam_tip: Mention that the converse is false: Dirichlet's function modified to take values $\pm 1$ has $|f|=1$ integrable, but $f$ is not integrable.

question: Let $f(x) = c$ be a constant function on $[a, b]$. Show that $f$ is Riemann integrable and $\int_a^b c dx = c(b-a)$.
approach: Compute $U(P, c)$ and $L(P, c)$ for an arbitrary partition $P$.

solution_steps.title: Extrema on Subintervals
solution_steps.math: f(x) = c \; \forall x \in [a, b] \implies M_i = c, \quad m_i = c \quad \forall i = 1, \dots, n
solution_steps.explanation: A constant function attains the same value everywhere.

solution_steps.title: Upper and Lower Sums
solution_steps.math: U(P, f) = \sum_{i=1}^n c \Delta x_i = c \sum_{i=1}^n \Delta x_i = c(b - a), \qquad L(P, f) = \sum_{i=1}^n c \Delta x_i = c(b - a)
solution_steps.explanation: The sum of the lengths of the subintervals is $\sum \Delta x_i = b - a$.

solution_steps.title: Conclusion
solution_steps.math: L(P, f) = U(P, f) = c(b - a) \implies \underline{\int_a^b} c dx = \overline{\int_a^b} c dx = c(b - a)
solution_steps.explanation: Since upper and lower sums are equal to $c(b-a)$ for every partition $P$, $f$ is integrable with integral $c(b-a)$.

final_answer: $f(x) = c$ is Riemann integrable and $\int_a^b c dx = c(b-a)$.
exam_tip: Notice this works for any constant $c$, whether positive, negative, or zero.

question: Show that if $P^*$ is a refinement of a partition $P$, then $L(P, f) \le L(P^*, f)$ and $U(P^*, f) \le U(P, f)$.
approach: Prove for adding a single partition point $x^*$, then use induction for any refinement $P^* \supseteq P$.

solution_steps.title: Single Point Refinement
solution_steps.math: P^* = P \cup \{x^*\}, \quad x^* \in (x_{k-1}, x_k)
solution_steps.explanation: The subinterval $[x_{k-1}, x_k]$ is split into $[x_{k-1}, x^*]$ and $[x^*, x_k]$.

solution_steps.title: Lower Sum Comparison
solution_steps.math: m_k' = \inf_{[x_{k-1}, x^*]} f \ge m_k, \quad m_k'' = \inf_{[x^*, x_k]} f \ge m_k
solution_steps.explanation: Since infimum over a subset is greater than or equal to infimum over the whole set.

solution_steps.title: Contribution Difference
solution_steps.explanation: Summing across all intervals gives $L(P^*, f) \ge L(P, f)$.

solution_steps.title: Upper Sum Comparison
solution_steps.math: M_k' \le M_k, \, M_k'' \le M_k \implies U(P^*, f) \le U(P, f)
solution_steps.explanation: Supremum over a subset is less than or equal to supremum over the whole set.

final_answer: $L(P, f) \le L(P^*, f)$ and $U(P^*, f) \le U(P, f)$ for any refinement $P^* \supseteq P$.
exam_tip: Mention the geometric intuition: refining adds more rectangles, filling gaps for lower sums and cutting corners for upper sums.

question: Show that every step function on $[a, b]$ is Riemann integrable.
approach: Use the fact that a step function is constant on open subintervals, which can be modified at finitely many endpoints without affecting integrability.

solution_steps.title: Step Function Definition
solution_steps.math: \phi(x) = c_i \quad \forall x \in (x_{i-1}, x_i), \quad i = 1, \dots, n
solution_steps.explanation: Where $P = \{x_0, x_1, \dots, x_n\}$ is the defining partition.

solution_steps.title: Linear Combination of Characteristic Functions
solution_steps.math: \phi(x) = \sum_{i=1}^n c_i \mathbf{1}_{(x_{i-1}, x_i)}(x) + \sum_{i=0}^n \phi(x_i) \mathbf{1}_{\{x_i\}}(x)
solution_steps.explanation: Characteristic functions of open intervals are Riemann integrable, and finite points of jump do not affect integrability.

solution_steps.title: Darboux Criterion / Evaluation
solution_steps.math: \int_a^b \phi(x) dx = \sum_{i=1}^n c_i (x_i - x_{i-1})
solution_steps.explanation: By additivity over subintervals, each interval contributes $c_i \Delta x_i$.

final_answer: Every step function is Riemann integrable with $\int_a^b \phi = \sum_{i=1}^n c_i \Delta x_i$.
exam_tip: Step functions form a dense subspace of $\mathcal{R}[a, b]$ in the $L^1$ norm.

question: Prove that if $f$ is Riemann integrable on $[a, b]$ and $c \in (a, b)$, then $f$ is integrable on $[a, c]$ and $[c, b]$ and $\int_a^b f = \int_a^c f + \int_c^b f$.
approach: Include $c$ in partitions of $[a, b]$, splitting $P = P_1 \cup P_2$ with $P_1$ partitioning $[a, c]$ and $P_2$ partitioning $[c, b]$.

solution_steps.title: Partition Splitting
solution_steps.math: P_1 \text{ partition of } [a, c], \; P_2 \text{ partition of } [c, b] \implies P = P_1 \cup P_2 \text{ partition of } [a, b]
solution_steps.explanation: The point $c$ serves as the right endpoint of $P_1$ and left endpoint of $P_2$.

solution_steps.title: Darboux Sum Additivity
solution_steps.math: U(P, f) = U(P_1, f) + U(P_2, f) \quad \text{and} \quad L(P, f) = L(P_1, f) + L(P_2, f)
solution_steps.explanation: The sum splits cleanly across the junction $c$.

solution_steps.title: Integrability Squeeze
solution_steps.math: U(P, f) - L(P, f) = [U(P_1, f) - L(P_1, f)] + [U(P_2, f) - L(P_2, f)] < \epsilon
solution_steps.explanation: Since each term is non-negative, $U(P_1, f) - L(P_1, f) < \epsilon$ and $U(P_2, f) - L(P_2, f) < \epsilon$.

solution_steps.title: Integral Equality
solution_steps.math: \int_a^b f = \int_a^c f + \int_c^b f
solution_steps.explanation: Taking infima/suprema proves the identity.

final_answer: If $f \in \mathcal{R}[a, b]$ and $c \in (a, b)$, then $f$ is integrable on $[a, c]$ and $[c, b]$, and $\int_a^b f = \int_a^c f + \int_c^b f$.
exam_tip: Note this identity extends to any ordering of $a, b, c$ using the convention $\int_b^a f = -\int_a^b f$.

question: Show that if $f: [a, b] \to \mathbb{R}$ is Riemann integrable, then $f$ is bounded on $[a, b]$.
approach: Proof by contradiction: if $f$ is unbounded, then in any partition at least one subinterval has $f$ unbounded, making Riemann sums diverge.

solution_steps.title: Assumption for Contradiction
solution_steps.math: f \in \mathcal{R}[a, b] \text{ with integral } L, \quad \text{suppose } f \text{ is unbounded on } [a, b]
solution_steps.explanation: Assume $f$ is Riemann integrable in the Riemann-sum sense, yet unbounded.

solution_steps.title: Riemann Sum Bound
solution_steps.math: \exists P = \{x_0, \dots, x_n\} : |S(\dot{P}, f) - L| < 1 \implies |S(\dot{P}, f)| < |L| + 1
solution_steps.explanation: For any choice of tags $t_i \in [x_{i-1}, x_i]$.

solution_steps.title: Unbounded Subinterval
solution_steps.math: \exists k \in \{1, \dots, n\} \text{ such that } f \text{ is unbounded on } [x_{k-1}, x_k]
solution_steps.explanation: If every subinterval were bounded, the entire interval $[a, b]$ would be bounded.

solution_steps.title: Contradiction via Tag Choice
solution_steps.math: S(\dot{P}, f) = f(t_k)\Delta x_k + \sum_{i \ne k} f(t_i)\Delta x_i \implies |f(t_k)|\Delta x_k \le |L| + 1 + \left|\sum_{i \ne k} f(t_i)\Delta x_i\right|
solution_steps.explanation: Since $f$ is unbounded on $[x_{k-1}, x_k]$, we can pick $t_k$ to make $|f(t_k)|$ arbitrarily large, violating the bound.

final_answer: If $f$ is Riemann integrable on $[a, b]$, then $f$ must be bounded on $[a, b]$.
exam_tip: This fundamental result explains why the Riemann integral cannot handle unbounded functions (which require improper integrals).

question: Evaluate $\lim_{n \to \infty} \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{n}{n^2 + i^2}$ by expressing it as a Riemann sum.
concept_tested: Evaluation of Limit of a Sum via Riemann Integral
approach: Rewrite $\sum_{i=1}^n \frac{n}{n^2 + i^2} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{1}{1 + (i/n)^2}$, recognize as Riemann sum of $f(x) = \frac{1}{1+x^2}$ on $[0, 1]$.

solution_steps.title: Algebraic Transformation
solution_steps.math: \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{n}{n^2 + i^2} = \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{n}{n^2\left(1 + \frac{i^2}{n^2}\right)} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{1}{1 + \left(\frac{i}{n}\right)^2}
solution_steps.explanation: Factor out $n^2$ from the denominator.

solution_steps.title: Identification as Riemann Sum
solution_steps.math: f(x) = \frac{1}{1+x^2}, \quad x_i = \frac{i}{n}, \quad \Delta x = \frac{1}{n} \implies \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n f\left(\frac{i}{n}\right) = \int_0^1 \frac{1}{1+x^2} dx
solution_steps.explanation: Since $f(x) = \frac{1}{1+x^2}$ is continuous on $[0, 1]$, the Riemann sums converge to the definite integral.

solution_steps.title: Evaluate the Integral
solution_steps.math: \int_0^1 \frac{1}{1+x^2} dx = [\arctan(x)]_0^1 = \arctan(1) - \arctan(0) = \frac{\pi}{4} - 0 = \frac{\pi}{4}
solution_steps.explanation: Standard antiderivative of $\frac{1}{1+x^2}$ is $\arctan(x)$.

exam_tip: Always write down the general formula: $\lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n f(i/n) = \int_0^1 f(x) dx$.

question: State and prove the First Mean Value Theorem for Integrals.
concept_tested: First Mean Value Theorem for Integrals (Past Paper Model)
approach: State and prove that for continuous $f$ on $[a, b]$, $\exists c \in [a, b]$ such that $\int_a^b f(x)dx = f(c)(b-a)$.

solution_steps.title: Statement
solution_steps.math: f: [a, b] \to \mathbb{R} \text{ is continuous} \implies \exists c \in [a, b] \text{ such that } \int_a^b f(x) dx = f(c)(b - a)
solution_steps.explanation: The average value of a continuous function on $[a, b]$ is attained at least once.

solution_steps.title: Extreme Value Theorem
solution_steps.math: m = \min_{x \in [a, b]} f(x), \quad M = \max_{x \in [a, b]} f(x) \implies m \le f(x) \le M \; (\forall x \in [a, b])
solution_steps.explanation: Continuous function on compact interval attains its minimum $m$ and maximum $M$.

solution_steps.title: Integrating the Inequalities
solution_steps.math: \int_a^b m dx \le \int_a^b f(x) dx \le \int_a^b M dx \implies m(b - a) \le \int_a^b f(x) dx \le M(b - a)
solution_steps.explanation: Since $b - a > 0$, divide by $b - a$.

solution_steps.title: Intermediate Value Theorem Application
solution_steps.math: m \le \frac{1}{b - a} \int_a^b f(x) dx \le M \implies \exists c \in [a, b] \text{ s.t. } f(c) = \frac{1}{b - a} \int_a^b f(x) dx
solution_steps.explanation: By IVT, $f$ takes on every value between its minimum $m$ and maximum $M$.

exam_tip: Combining EVT (Extreme Value Theorem) and IVT (Intermediate Value Theorem) is the classic proof.
